title: Strong Passwords and Online Safety
summary: Why weak passwords are easy to guess, how to build strong passwords and passphrases, and how secrecy, two-step verification, and spotting fake messages keep accounts safe.
poll: A long password is more important than a complicated one.

versions.title: Keep Your Password Safe
versions.text:
Say you have a game you love. To get in, you type a secret word. It is a password. It keeps your account safe. An account is your own space in an app.

Some kids pick bad ones. They use 123456. They use their name. Bad guys can guess these fast. They use a tool. It tries lots of words each second.

A strong password is long. Long ones are hard to guess. Mix big and small letters. Add a number. Add a symbol, like # or !. Or join three or four words that do not fit, like camel, lamp, and moon.

Do not use one password on each site. If one gets out, the rest are not safe.

Keep it a secret. Do not tell a friend. Your mom or dad can know it.

Some sites send a code to a phone, too. You need the code and the password to get in. That helps a lot.

Watch out for fake notes. A note may say, "Send us your password!" A real site will not ask. Do not click. Tell a grown-up.

On a shared computer, log out when you are done.

versions.title: Strong Passwords and Online Safety
versions.text:
Imagine you want to play your favorite online game. Before you can begin, you type a secret word called a password. It protects your account, which is your own personal space in an app or on a website.

Many people choose weak passwords, like 123456 or their own name. Hackers can guess these very quickly. They use computer programs that can try millions of guesses every second.

A strong password is long, because longer passwords are much harder to guess. Mix capital and small letters, and add numbers and symbols, such as # or !. You can also join several words that do not belong together, like camel, lantern, mango, and cloud. This is called a passphrase, and it is easy to remember.

Never use the same password for every website. If one password is stolen, all your other accounts are in danger, too.

Keep your password a secret. Do not share it with friends, even your best friend. Only your parents should know it.

Some websites also send a special code to a phone. You need both the code and the password to get in. This extra step is called two-step verification, and it helps keep hackers out.

Watch out for scam messages. A message may say, "Send us your password!" Real companies will never ask for it. Do not click the link, and tell a trusted adult.

When you use a shared computer, always remember to log out when you finish.

versions.title: Strong Passwords and Online Safety
versions.text:
Imagine you want to play your favorite online game. Before you can begin, you type a secret word called a password. A password protects your account, which is your own personal space on a website or app where your messages and progress are saved.

Many people choose weak passwords, such as 123456, the word password, or their own name. Hackers can guess these very quickly, because they use computer programs that try millions of guesses every second.

A strong password is long, since longer passwords are much harder to guess. Mixing capital and small letters, numbers, and symbols such as # or ! makes it even stronger. Another smart choice is a passphrase, which joins several unrelated words, like camel, lantern, mango, and cloud. A passphrase is easy for you to remember but hard for a computer to guess.

Never use the same password for every account. If one website is hacked and your password is stolen, criminals can try it on all your other accounts.

Keep your passwords secret. Do not share them with friends, even your best friend. Only a parent or guardian should know them.

Many websites also offer two-step verification. They send a special code to a phone, and you need both the code and the password to sign in. Even if a hacker learns your password, the code keeps them out.

Be careful of scam messages that pretend to come from real companies and ask for your password. Real companies never ask for it, so do not click, and tell a trusted adult. On a shared computer, always log out when you finish.

Keep your passwords private, and do not share them with friends, even your closest friend. Only a parent or guardian should know them.

versions.title: Locking Your Digital Door: Passwords and Safety
versions.text:
Imagine you want to play your favorite online game. Before you can begin, you type a secret combination of characters called a password, which protects your account. An account is your personal space on a website or application, where your messages, files, and progress are stored.

Unfortunately, many people select weak passwords, such as 123456, the word password, or their own name and birthday, and these choices are dangerously easy to discover. Hackers can guess these almost instantly, because they use automated programs that attempt millions of combinations every second.

A strong password is long, since longer passwords are considerably more difficult to guess. Combining uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols such as # or ! makes a password even stronger. Another practical option is a passphrase, which combines several unrelated words, like camel, lantern, mango, and cloud, so that it is easy for a person to remember but difficult for a computer to predict.

Never reuse the same password for multiple accounts, because if one website is hacked and your password is stolen, criminals can immediately test it on all your other accounts as well.

Keep your passwords confidential, and do not share them with friends, even your closest friend. Only a parent or guardian should know them.

Many websites also provide two-step verification, which sends a temporary code to a phone. You need both the code and the password to sign in, so even if a hacker discovers your password, the code prevents the hacker from entering.

Be cautious of phishing, a type of scam in which criminals send messages that pretend to come from legitimate companies and request your password. Genuine companies never ask for it this way, so avoid clicking any links, and inform a trusted adult. On a shared computer at school or in a library, always log out when you finish.

versions.title: Locking Your Digital Door: Passwords and Safety
versions.text:
Whenever you open a favorite game or a school platform, you probably type a password, a secret combination of characters that works as the key to your account. An account is the personal space that stores your information, conversations, and progress on a particular website or application.

Unfortunately, many people select predictable passwords, such as 123456, the word password, or their own name and birthday. Hackers frequently use automated programs that can attempt millions of combinations every second, so a short or obvious password may be discovered almost instantly.

Security experts explain that length is the most important feature of a strong password, because every additional character greatly increases the number of possible combinations. Combining uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols such as # or ! makes guessing even harder. Another practical approach is a passphrase, a string of several unrelated words, such as camel, lantern, mango, and cloud, which is easy for a person to remember but difficult for a computer to predict.

Reusing one password for multiple accounts is especially risky. If one website suffers a data breach, criminals can immediately try the stolen password on every other service you use, including your email and games.

Passwords should remain confidential. You may share them with a parent or guardian who helps protect you online, but not with friends, no matter how trustworthy they seem, because even good friends can make careless mistakes.

Many services also offer two-step verification, which requires a temporary code, usually sent to a phone, in addition to the password. Therefore, even an attacker who has stolen your password cannot enter the account without that code.

Finally, beware of phishing, a trick in which criminals send fake messages that imitate real companies and ask for your password or urge you to click a link. Genuine organizations never request your password this way, so avoid clicking, report the message to a trusted adult, and always log out after using a shared computer at school or in a library.

versions.title: Locking Your Digital Door: Passwords and Safety
versions.text:
Whenever you open a favorite game, a school platform, or a messaging application, you probably type a password, a confidential sequence of characters that functions as the key to your account. An account is the personal space that stores your information, conversations, and progress on a particular website or service.

Unfortunately, many people select predictable passwords, such as 123456, the word password itself, or their own name and birthday, and these choices are extraordinarily vulnerable. Hackers frequently employ automated programs that can attempt millions or even billions of combinations every second, so a short or obvious password may be discovered almost instantly.

Security experts emphasize that length is the most significant characteristic of a strong password, because every additional character multiplies the number of possible combinations that an attacker must test. Combining uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols such as # or ! increases the difficulty further. An even more practical approach is a passphrase, a string of several unrelated words, such as camel, lantern, mango, and cloud, which is easy for a person to remember but remarkably difficult for a computer to predict.

Reusing a single password across multiple accounts is particularly hazardous. If one website suffers a data breach, criminals can immediately try the stolen password on every other service you use, and one mistake can then expose your entire online life.

Passwords should remain confidential. You may share them with a parent or guardian who helps you stay safe, but not with friends, regardless of how trustworthy those friends appear to be.

Many services also offer two-step verification, which requires a temporary code, typically delivered to a phone, in addition to the password itself. As a result, even an attacker who has obtained your password cannot enter the account without that second piece of evidence.

Finally, beware of phishing, a deceptive technique in which criminals send counterfeit messages that imitate legitimate companies and request your password or urge you to click a suspicious link. Genuine organizations never ask for your password in this manner, so you should avoid clicking, report the message to a trusted adult, and delete it. When you finish using a shared computer at school or in a library, always remember to log out completely.

HIGH.prompt: Imagine you are writing advice for students who are getting their first school account. Explain the three most important password habits from the article and why each one matters.

HIGH.modelAnswer: The first habit is creating a long passphrase made of several unrelated words, such as camel, lantern, mango, and cloud, because adding more characters makes it nearly impossible for a hacker's program to guess. The second habit is turning on two-step verification, which requires both a password and a code sent to your phone, so even if a phishing message tricks someone into revealing their password, the hacker still cannot get in. The third habit is never reusing one password across accounts, since a password stolen from one site could unlock every other account. Together, a strong passphrase, verification, and unique passwords protect a brand-new school account from the very first day.
